segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had finished these sayings, he left Galilee and came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some Pharisees came to him to test him, asking,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is it permitted for a man to divorce his wife for any reason whatever?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you not read that the Creator from the beginning ‘made them male and female’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, then, let no human being separate.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then did Moses command us to give a certificate of dismissal and divorce her?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It was because of your hardness of heart that Moses permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I tell you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If that is how things stand between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by people, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of the heavens. Let the one who can accept it accept it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray, but the disciples rebuked them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let the children be, and do not stop them from coming to me, for the kingdom of the heavens belongs to such as these.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after laying his hands on them, he went on from there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then someone came up to him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, what good thing must I do to have eternal life?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which ones?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not give false testimony,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The young man said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I have observed. What do I still lack?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If you want to be complete, go, sell what you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens. Then come, follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the young man heard this saying, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who then can be saved?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus looked at them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter said to him in reply,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, at the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundred times as much and will inherit eternal life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

notes.note: The question reflects a live debate over the grounds for divorce in Deuteronomy 24:1. Later rabbinic sources record that the school of Shammai limited divorce to sexual misconduct, while the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any cause. The Pharisees are asking Jesus to take a side; the phrase could also be read more narrowly as 'for every kind of reason'.

The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual activity, and its exact scope here is disputed. Most interpreters take it to mean adultery or sexual unfaithfulness by the wife. Others limit it to unchastity before marriage, or to marriages within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18. The broad English term leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

notes.phrase: and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery
notes.note: This final clause is absent from some important early manuscripts and is omitted by several modern critical editions and translations. Those editions regard it as an addition by copyists influenced by Matthew 5:32. The SBLGNT, followed here, includes it.

It is unclear which saying is meant. It may be the disciples' remark that it is better not to marry, in which case Jesus grants that celibacy is a gift for some. It may instead be his own teaching on marriage and divorce in verses 4–9. Most interpreters prefer the first, since verse 12 goes on to speak of those who forgo marriage.

Eunuchs were a familiar class in the ancient world, some of them castrated to serve in royal courts. The third group is almost universally understood as a figure of speech for those who choose to remain unmarried for the sake of God's kingdom. It is not taken as a reference to physical self-mutilation.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that follows Hebrew and Aramaic usage and is characteristic of Matthew. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed it; the phrase means the same as 'the kingdom of God' in verse 24.

In Jewish usage of the period, 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, the era of God's reign that follows the present age. The phrase concerns the kind of life as well as its unending length, which is why Jesus can call it simply 'life' in verse 17. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

notes.phrase: Why do you ask me about what is good?
notes.traditional: Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God
notes.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'Good Teacher' in verse 16 and 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God' here. That wording matches the parallel accounts in Mark 10 and Luke 18. The earliest manuscripts of Matthew have the form translated here, and the longer form is generally regarded as a harmonization by copyists.

The Greek word describes something that has reached its goal: whole, mature, lacking nothing. In the Greek Old Testament it translates Hebrew words for wholehearted or undivided devotion. 'Perfect', the usual rendering, now suggests flawlessness. 'Complete' also answers the young man's question directly: he asked what he still lacks.

The saying is deliberate exaggeration: the largest animal familiar in the region set against the smallest opening. The popular explanation that 'the Needle's Eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence behind it. The disciples' astonishment and Jesus' word 'impossible' in verse 26 show that a literal needle is meant.

The single Greek word means 'rebirth' or 'renewal'. Greek and Jewish writers of the period used it for the restoration of the world or of a nation after catastrophe. Here it refers to the new order of the age to come, when God sets the world right; 'of all things' is supplied to make that cosmic sense clear, as most modern translations do.
Some early manuscripts lack 'or wife', and several modern critical editions omit the words as a copyist's addition drawn from Luke 18:29. The SBLGNT includes them and is followed here.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul and Revelation, and translators vary between 'fornication', 'sexual immorality', 'unchastity' and 'prostitution', so the exception clauses and vice lists need one decision.
Occurs in Matthew 5:48, Paul, Hebrews and James, where 'perfect', 'mature' and 'complete' compete, and 'perfect' misleads modern readers toward flawlessness.
Jesus' introductory formula occurs dozens of times in all four Gospels, and it should not vary between 'truly', 'amen', 'I assure you' and 'verily'.
The verb covers rescue, healing and final salvation across the New Testament, so a policy is needed on when to use 'save', 'heal' or 'rescue'.
In the marriage sense translators vary between 'divorce', 'put away', 'dismiss' and 'send away' across Matthew 1, 5 and 19, Mark 10 and Luke 16, and readers need the divorce sayings to match.
